column_1: General notes applicable to all tables

This worksheet contains important background notes on the data as well as some table specific notes and explanation of the shorthand used. There are three tables vertically aligned in columns A and B.

column_2: Note text

Statistics presented in these tables are for work-related fatal injuries in Great Britain reportable under the Reporting of Injuries, Diseases and Dangerous Occurrences Regulations (RIDDOR).  For more information on RIDDOR see www.hse.gov.uk/statistics/sources.htm.

Table 1 and Tables 3-5 present annual reportable fatal injury statistics to workers (employees and self-employed) for the 5 years 2021/22 - 2025/26 along with the latest five-year total. The number of fatal injuries for some groupings are relatively small and are susceptible to considerable year-on-year variation so figures presented in the table need to be interpreted with care, particularly with respect to trends over time. The five-year rate essentially averages out the rate, smoothing out this year-on-year variation.

Table 2 presents the number of annual reportable fatal injuries to Members of the Public for the 5 years 2021/22 - 2025/26 and includes deaths as a result of a work-related accident, though the injured person was 'not at work' themselves. It should be noted that these statistics of deaths to members of the public arising from work-related activities do not include such incidents to 'patient and service users' in England for premises registered with Care Quality Commission (CQC)

Rates of injury: Differences in the size of the workforce will impact on comparisons of the number of fatal injuries, both over time and between one group and another within a year (e.g. between different industry groups).  In order to make comparisons between groups it is important to consider the rate of fatal injury.  The rate is constructed by dividing the count of injuries by the employment estimate.  This is then multiplied by a factor of 100,000 to give a rate per 100,000 workers, in line with international standards. The source of employment data used to construct the injury rates from 2004/05 onwards is the Annual Population Survey (APS). For more information see https://www.hse.gov.uk/statistics/assets/docs/sources.pdf. The rates are expressed to two decimal places.
For more information on statistics of work-related fatal injuries, see https://www.hse.gov.uk/statistics/fatals-overview.htm.

Figures for 2025/26 are at this stage provisional and are marked as 'p' in the tables.  They will be finalised in July 2027 following any necessary adjustments.  Figures for 2024/25 have been revised (finalised) and are marked as 'r' in the tables. The number of deaths in 2024/25 increased by 8 (4 workers and 4 members of the public) between the provisional and revised count. More details can be found in the revision log.

Numbers for 2021/22 are affected by the impacts of the coronavirus pandemic. This should be considered when comparing across time periods. For more details see our reports on the impact of the coronavirus pandemic on health and safety statistics.

The employment data used to calculate rates includes those temporarily absent from work. In 2021/22 the number of such workers was higher than previous years due to temporary employment schemes (e.g. furlough) introduced during the coronavirus pandemic. This has contributed to a discontinuity in injury rates.
